relationshipLegend.exact: Same named instrument in its home institution.
relationshipLegend.exact-concept: Same institutional concept, not necessarily the same instrument.
relationshipLegend.exact-example: A direct example of the concept.
relationshipLegend.similar-function: Performs a materially similar operational function, but design may differ.
relationshipLegend.related: Related mechanism or policy tool; not an equivalent.
relationshipLegend.no-direct-equivalent: No sufficiently close direct operational equivalent.

entries.name: Standing Facility
entries.definition: A permanent central-bank facility that eligible counterparties can access on their own initiative, usually to borrow or place funds overnight.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Do not treat every standing facility as an emergency facility or assume facilities across central banks are economically identical.

entries.name: Deposit Facility
entries.definition: An overnight facility through which eligible institutions place funds with a central bank at a specified rate.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: A deposit facility is not automatically the same as paying interest on all reserve balances.

entries.name: Marginal Lending Facility
entries.definition: An overnight collateralised borrowing facility that gives eligible banks access to central-bank liquidity at a posted rate.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Functional similarity does not imply identical counterparties, collateral, pricing or stigma.

entries.name: Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB)
entries.definition: Interest paid by the Federal Reserve on balances maintained by eligible institutions at Federal Reserve Banks.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: IORB is not a universal deposit facility for every money-market participant.

translations.term: Bank Rate paid on eligible reserves

entries.name: Overnight Reverse Repo Facility (ON RRP)
entries.definition: A Federal Reserve operation that accepts overnight cash from eligible counterparties against securities and helps place a floor under money-market rates.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: ON RRP and IORB work together but serve different eligible counterparty sets.

entries.name: Standing Repo Facility
entries.definition: A standing Federal Reserve repo facility that supplies overnight liquidity against eligible securities and helps limit upward pressure on overnight funding rates.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: A repo facility is not identical to an unsecured central-bank loan.

entries.name: Main Refinancing Operation (MRO)
entries.definition: A regular Eurosystem liquidity-providing operation used in monetary-policy implementation.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: MRO is a specific Eurosystem instrument, not a generic name for every central-bank repo.

entries.name: Longer-Term Refinancing Operation (LTRO)
entries.definition: A Eurosystem refinancing operation that supplies central-bank liquidity for maturities longer than the regular main refinancing operation.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: LTRO and TLTRO should not be used interchangeably; targeted operations can carry additional conditions.

entries.name: Targeted Longer-Term Refinancing Operation (TLTRO)
entries.definition: A Eurosystem longer-term funding operation whose terms are linked to specified lending conditions or objectives.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Similar policy intent does not make targeted funding schemes operationally equivalent.

entries.name: Minimum Reserve Requirements
entries.definition: Rules requiring specified institutions to hold a minimum amount of reserves with the central bank over a defined maintenance framework.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: A zero reserve-requirement ratio does not mean banks hold zero reserves.

translations.term: No direct equivalent in current framework

entries.name: Reserve Averaging
entries.definition: A framework that allows institutions to satisfy reserve requirements on average over a maintenance period rather than at every instant.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Averaging changes the timing flexibility of reserve holdings; it does not eliminate reserve requirements.

entries.name: Excess Reserves
entries.definition: Reserve balances held above a binding required amount, where such a requirement exists.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: The term can become misleading when reserve requirements are zero or the operating framework changes.

translations.term: Excess reserves / reserve holdings above minimum
Reserve balances; 'excess reserves' is less useful under zero requirements

entries.name: Ample-Reserves Regime
entries.definition: An operating regime in which aggregate reserve supply is high enough that small changes in reserves do not materially push the overnight policy rate away from its target.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Ample does not mean infinite: reserve demand can shift and scarcity can emerge at the margin.

entries.name: Scarce-Reserves Regime
entries.definition: A regime in which reserve supply is tight enough that marginal changes in reserves have a stronger effect on overnight funding rates.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Scarcity is an operational condition, not simply a low absolute reserve number.

entries.name: Floor System
entries.definition: A framework in which the rate paid on central-bank balances or a related facility helps anchor overnight market rates near a lower policy boundary.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Real-world systems can be hybrid; labels should not replace institution-specific rules.

entries.name: Corridor System
entries.definition: A framework in which a lending rate and deposit rate form upper and lower boundaries around a targeted overnight market rate.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: A corridor can coexist with abundant liquidity; observed trading may sit near one edge rather than the midpoint.

entries.name: Policy Rate Corridor
entries.definition: The range between central-bank lending and deposit-type rates that helps bound overnight money-market rates.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: The headline policy rate need not sit mechanically at the centre of every corridor.

translations.term: Marginal lending rate ↔ deposit facility rate

entries.name: Autonomous Factors
entries.definition: Central-bank balance-sheet items outside routine monetary-policy operations that mechanically add to or drain banking-system liquidity.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: These factors can move reserves without a new monetary-policy decision.

translations.term: Non-reserve liabilities / Treasury General Account / currency
Banknotes, government deposits and other balance-sheet factors

entries.name: Government Deposit Drain
entries.definition: A fall in banking-system reserves that occurs when private-sector payments move into a government account held at the central bank, all else equal.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: This is a balance-sheet transmission mechanism, not proof of deliberate monetary tightening.

entries.name: Liquidity Injection
entries.definition: An operation or balance-sheet movement that increases central-bank money available to eligible financial institutions.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: A liquidity injection is not automatically fiscal stimulus or permanent money creation.

entries.name: Liquidity Absorption
entries.definition: An operation or balance-sheet movement that removes or immobilises central-bank liquidity from the banking system.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Absorption can be temporary and does not necessarily signal a change in the policy stance.

entries.name: Sterilisation
entries.definition: An offsetting operation designed to neutralise the liquidity effect of another central-bank transaction or balance-sheet flow.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Sterilisation addresses the liquidity consequence of an action, not necessarily its other market effects.

entries.name: Fine-Tuning Operation
entries.definition: An operation used to manage unexpected liquidity fluctuations or short-term interest-rate pressures between regular operations.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: The term is institution-specific; not every ad hoc operation is formally a fine-tuning operation.

entries.name: Fixed-Rate Full Allotment
entries.definition: A tender format in which eligible counterparties can obtain the amount they request at a fixed rate, subject to collateral and operational rules.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Full allotment does not mean unsecured or unlimited access.

entries.name: Eligible Collateral
entries.definition: Assets that satisfy a central bank's rules for use in collateralised credit or liquidity operations.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Eligibility is facility-specific and can change; an asset being eligible does not imply zero credit risk.

entries.name: Collateral Haircut
entries.definition: A valuation deduction applied to collateral so that the credit extended is lower than the collateral's market or assessed value.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Haircuts are risk controls, not market-price forecasts.

entries.name: Counterparty Eligibility
entries.definition: The institutional and operational requirements determining which entities may access a particular central-bank operation or facility.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Eligibility can differ sharply across facilities at the same central bank.

entries.name: Repurchase Agreement (Repo)
entries.definition: A collateralised financing transaction structured as a sale of securities with an agreement to reverse the transaction later.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Market naming conventions differ: central-bank 'repo' direction can be described from the central bank or counterparty perspective.

entries.name: Reverse Repo
entries.definition: The opposite side of a repo transaction; in central-bank implementation it is commonly used to absorb cash from counterparties.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Always check whose perspective defines 'repo' versus 'reverse repo'.

entries.name: Outright Asset Purchase
entries.definition: A purchase in which the central bank acquires a security without a contractual near-term reversal.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: An outright purchase differs fundamentally from a repo because it has no pre-agreed reversal transaction.

entries.name: Balance-Sheet Runoff
entries.definition: A decline in central-bank securities holdings as assets mature, are redeemed, or are otherwise allowed to leave the portfolio without full reinvestment.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Runoff is not the same as actively selling securities.

entries.name: Reinvestment
entries.definition: Using principal payments from maturing central-bank holdings to purchase replacement assets and maintain some or all of a portfolio.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Reinvestment policy can matter even when the headline policy rate is unchanged.

entries.name: Reserve Creation
entries.definition: An increase in commercial-bank reserve balances generated by central-bank transactions, such as asset purchases or lending, subject to offsetting balance-sheet flows.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Central-bank reserve creation is not the same as creating household bank deposits in every transaction.

translations.term: Current account balances at the Bank

entries.name: Reserve Scarcity Signal
entries.definition: A market indicator suggesting that reserves are becoming more valuable at the margin, often visible through overnight funding spreads, facility use or rate sensitivity.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: No single indicator proves scarcity; the signal should be interpreted as a bundle.

translations.term: Reserve demand and short-term rate pressure

entries.name: Facility Usage
entries.definition: The amount borrowed from or placed into a central-bank facility over a specified period.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Usage can reflect pricing, market structure, regulation or operational convenience—not only stress.

entries.name: Overnight Rate Drift
entries.definition: A persistent movement of an overnight market rate toward one side of the central bank's intended operating range.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Small movements can be normal; interpretation depends on the framework and maintenance cycle.

entries.name: Collateral Scarcity
entries.definition: A condition in which particular high-quality securities become unusually valuable for financing or settlement, affecting repo pricing and market functioning.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Collateral scarcity is distinct from a shortage of central-bank reserves.

entries.name: Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF)
entries.definition: A PBoC lending operation that provides medium-term funding to eligible financial institutions against collateral and has historically played a role in China's monetary-policy implementation.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: MLF should not be translated mechanically into an ECB LTRO; institutional design and policy signalling differ.

entries.name: Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRR)
entries.definition: The required share of specified deposits that banks must hold as reserves under China's reserve-requirement framework.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: An RRR change affects structural liquidity conditions but is not equivalent to a policy-rate change.

entries.name: PBoC Open Market Operations
entries.definition: Market operations used by the People's Bank of China to add or absorb short-term liquidity, commonly through repo-style instruments.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Identical labels across central banks do not imply identical instruments or operating frameworks.

entries.name: S$NEER Policy Band
entries.definition: Singapore's exchange-rate-centred monetary-policy framework, in which MAS manages the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate within a policy band rather than using a conventional short-term policy rate as its primary instrument.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Do not translate MAS policy into a conventional rate-hike/rate-cut framework.

entries.name: Cash Rate Corridor
entries.definition: The operational structure around the RBA cash-rate target in which standing remuneration and lending arrangements help guide the overnight cash rate.
entries.whatPeopleGetWrong: Corridor width and implementation details differ across central banks.
